Level 1 · Introduction · Week 9

Variables, Input and Choices

Programs can ask questions, remember the answers and decide what to do.

What you will learn

  • How a variable remembers a value.
  • How to ask a question with input, and turn the answer into a number with int.
  • How if, elif and else let a program choose.
  • Which questions a program should never ask.
Print this week (PDF, 50 KB) Starter files (ZIP)

The big idea: labeled boxes

Remember the score variable in Scratch? A variable is a box with a label. You put something in it, and you can use it later.

One equals sign = means put in the box. (Two equals signs == mean something else — see below!)

Asking a question

input asks a question in the Shell and waits. Click in the Shell, type your answer and press Return. But watch out: input always gives back text, even when you type a number.

answer = input("How big should the square be? ")
size = int(answer)

Exercise9.1: Square of Any Size

Folder: week09/ex-size-it. Run the starter and type 120 in the Shell. A red TypeError! The turtle cannot walk the text "120". Fix it with size = int(answer). Try 50, 150 and 250.

Making choices: if, elif, else

A program can choose what to do. Python checks the rules from the top. The first rule that is true wins, and the others are skipped. else catches everything that is left.

if color_name == "orange":
    color = "#E69F00"
elif color_name == "blue":
    color = "#0072B2"
else:
    print("I do not know that color. I will use black.")
    color = "#000000"

Every if, elif and else line ends with a colon, and the lines under it are pushed in 4 spaces — just like loops.

Comparing

Sign Means Example that is true
== is the same as "blue" == "blue"
!= is not the same as "Blue" != "blue" (Python is picky!)
< is less than 3 < 10
> is more than 25 > 10

Exercise9.2: Pick a Color

Folder: week09/ex-color-choice. The program knows orange and blue. Add an elif for "green" ("#009E73") and an else that prints a friendly message and uses black. Test with orange, blue, green and pizza. The color name is written under the circle, so you can tell the colors apart even without seeing color.

Exercise9.3: How Many Stars?

Folder: week09/ex-star-row. Ask how many stars (1 to 10). Before drawing: if the number is more than 10, print a message and use 10; elif it is less than 1, print a message and use 1; else print "Coming right up!". Test with 3, 25 and 0.

Questions a program should NOT ask

Check one box for each question.

Question OK Never
What is your favorite color? ☐ ☐
Where do you live? ☐ ☐
How many stars should I draw? ☐ ☐
What is your password? ☐ ☐
What is your hero name? ☐ ☐
What school do you go to? ☐ ☐
What is your full name? ☐ ☐
What is your favorite animal? ☐ ☐

Our rule: ask about choices (colors, sizes, numbers), never about who you are. If an app or game asks for personal details, stop and ask a grown-up.

Reflect

Think of a game you know. Where does it ask you something and then decide what happens?

Why does input need int for sizes, but not for color names?

New words

Variable
A labeled box that remembers a value, like size = 100 .
input
Asks a question in the Shell and gives back the answer as text.
int
Turns text like "120" into the number 120.
Text (string)
Letters or numbers inside quote marks, like "blue" or "120" .
if / elif / else
Python’s way to choose: “if this, else if that, otherwise…”
Comparison
A question with a yes/no answer, like stars > 10 .

Homework: Mini Math Quiz

15–20 minutes. Do Core first; Challenge and Creative are optional.

CoreMini Math Quiz (about 10 minutes)

Open week09/hw-math-quiz/starter.py. No turtle this time: everything happens in the Shell.

  1. Press Run and answer question 1 in the Shell. Read how it works: input, then int, then if/else, and score = score + 1 when the answer is right.

  2. Add question 2 the same way: “What is 9 + 15?” (the answer is 24).

  3. At the end, print the score: print("You scored", score, "out of 2").

No computer at home? Write question 2 here (copy the pattern of question 1):

ChallengePerfect score

Add a third question of your own. Change “out of 2” to “out of 3”. Then, at the very end, add an if that prints a special message when score == 3. Remember: two equals signs ask a question!

CreativeChoose your path

Write a tiny adventure: the program asks “You find a door and a tunnel. Which do you choose?” and uses if/elif/else to print a different ending for door, tunnel and anything else. Plan it here first:

Remember the rule: our programs ask about choices, never about who you are (no names, addresses, schools or passwords).
